d.try: Feel the bottom or back of a laptop or games console after an hour of use, without blocking its vents. Now picture thousands of those packed into one hall. Count how many apps on a family phone save things "to the cloud", and remember each one needs a server somewhere.
myth: Things saved "in the cloud" are floating somewhere in the sky or the air.
The cloud is just other people's computers. Your files sit on hard drives and memory chips inside real buildings, usually copied to more than one site in case a building fails.
facts: rows of servers in tall metal racks

sec.t:
Walk into a data hall and the first thing you notice is the noise: a loud, steady roar from thousands of fans. Each rack holds dozens of flat servers slotted in like books on a shelf. Bundles of cables run overhead or under a raised floor, carrying power and data.

Some servers do the thinking, with powerful chips. Others are mostly storage, crammed with hard drives or memory chips. Fibre-optic cables connect the building to the wider [[@internet-how|internet]], often through several different routes, so one cut cable doesn't knock everything offline. Security is tight. Many sites have fences, guards and fingerprint or card scanners at every door.

Almost every bit of electricity a server uses turns into heat. Packed together, servers would quickly overheat and break. So a large part of a data centre is really a giant cooling machine.

The usual trick is to arrange racks in "hot aisles" and "cold aisles". Cool air is blown in at the front of the servers and hot air leaves at the back, where it is pulled away. Big chillers work like an [[@air-conditioning|air conditioner]] the size of a house. Newer chips for artificial intelligence run so hot that some are cooled with liquid flowing through pipes right next to them.

{{story:air-conditioning}}

Location helps. Google's data centre at Hamina in Finland uses cold seawater from the Baltic. In hot places such as Chennai or Arizona, cooling costs more.

A data centre is expected to keep running even during [[@what-if-no-electricity|a power cut]]. Rooms full of [[@batteries|batteries]] take over instantly if the mains supply fails. Within seconds, diesel generators the size of a shipping container start up and keep the lights on for hours or days.

The biggest companies copy your data to several buildings, sometimes in different countries. If a flood or fire hits one, another takes over. That is why your photos don't vanish when one machine dies.

sec.h: Where they are, and the cost
sec.t:
Northern Virginia, near Washington DC, has more data centres than anywhere else on Earth, partly because some of the early internet's main connections met there. In India, Mumbai and Navi Mumbai host the largest share, helped by the [[@undersea-internet|undersea cables]] that land on the coast nearby. Chennai, Hyderabad and Delhi's surrounding region are growing fast.

All this uses a lot of power. The International Energy Agency estimates data centres used about 1.5% of the world's electricity in 2024, and expects that to rise quickly as artificial intelligence spreads. If that electricity comes from coal, it adds to [[@climate-change|climate change]]. So companies are signing deals for solar and wind power and trying to use less water for cooling. In parts of Scandinavia, the waste heat from servers is piped into homes to keep them warm in winter.

text: Chanakya was a Brahmin scholar who, according to tradition, lived around 300 BCE. He is said to have taught at Taxila, a famous centre of learning in what is now Pakistan.

The best-known story says he was insulted at the court of the Nanda king of Magadha and vowed to bring the dynasty down. He found a bright young man, Chandragupta, trained him and helped him take the throne. This began the [[@mauryan-empire|Mauryan Empire]]. Chanakya is also known as Kautilya, the name on a famous Sanskrit book about running a kingdom, the *Arthashastra*.

st.prompt: The Arthashastra gives a rule about which kingdoms are likely to be your enemies. Which one?

options.t: The kingdom right next to yours
The kingdom furthest away
Any kingdom with a bigger army

st.reveal: The book describes kingdoms as circles. Your neighbour is your natural rival, and your neighbour's neighbour is your natural friend. This "circle of kings" idea still comes up in talk about foreign policy.

R. Shamasastry, Kautilya's Arthashastra, English translation (1915).
n.certNote: Chanakya is known mostly from later stories, not from records of his own time. Many scholars think the Arthashastra, the book linked to him, was written and revised by several people over centuries.

myth: Chanakya wrote every word of the Arthashastra exactly as we read it today.
Tradition credits him, but the text we have seems to have been edited and added to over a long time. Many scholars think it took its final form a few centuries after the Mauryas.
facts: helping Chandragupta Maurya win the throne

sec.t:
For centuries, people knew the Arthashastra only from mentions in other works. Then, in 1905, a bundle of palm-leaf manuscripts was handed to the Oriental Library in Mysore. The librarian, R. Shamasastry, realised he was holding the lost text.

He published it in Sanskrit in 1909 and in English in 1915. Scholars around the world were startled. Here was a detailed handbook of government from ancient India, covering topics most people thought only modern states worried about. The find changed how historians saw early India. It showed that thinkers there had written carefully about money, law and power, as well as about religion and poetry.

Writers often compare Kautilya with Niccolò Machiavelli, an Italian who wrote *The Prince* in 1513, another blunt guide for rulers. Both describe power as it works, not as people wish it worked.

But the Arthashastra also says a king's happiness lies in the happiness of his people. It sets out rules for fair wages, punishments for officials who cheat and help for orphans and the old. So readers find both cold strategy and real concern for good government in it.

No inscription from his own time names him. The stories about his life come from Buddhist, Jain and Hindu texts written much later, and they disagree about details. A famous Sanskrit play, *Mudrarakshasa*, shows him outwitting a rival minister, but it was written many centuries after him.

Some scholars think Chanakya and Kautilya may have been joined into one figure over time. The book itself mentions earlier teachers and seems to have grown in stages. So the man is partly history and partly legend.

His name is everywhere in India. A collection of short sayings called *Chanakya Niti* is quoted in homes and offices, though it was put together long after him. In [[@delhi|Delhi]], the area where many embassies stand is called Chanakyapuri, a fitting name for a place full of diplomats.

TV serials and films have made him a hero of clever strategy. Students of politics around the world still read the Arthashastra as one of the oldest guides to statecraft.

text: Polynesian sailors found their way across the Pacific by reading nature. They steered by the rising and setting points of stars and felt the long ocean swells rolling under their canoes. They watched which way birds flew at dusk, and noticed clouds piling up over hidden islands.

They sailed in big double-hulled canoes, two hulls joined by a deck, with sails woven from pandanus leaves. These canoes could carry families, pigs, chickens, dogs and plants to start a new life. Food for the voyage included breadfruit, taro, coconuts and dried fish.

Over about 2,000 years, they spread across a huge triangle of ocean, from [[@hawaii-culture|Hawaiʻi]] in the north to [[@new-zealand|Aotearoa New Zealand]] in the south-west and Rapa Nui in the east. They reached almost every island where people could live.

st.prompt: Far out at sea, a Polynesian navigator spots a seabird called a tern flying home at dusk. What does that tell them?

options.t: Land is probably within a day's sail in that direction
A storm is coming in the next hour
The canoe is near the equator

st.reveal: Some seabirds fly out to fish in the morning and return to land at dusk, usually staying within about 30 to 50 km of home. Following them at sunset can point the way to an island.

src: Polynesian Voyaging Society, history of Hōkūleʻa.
Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Pacific voyaging and wayfinding.
Britannica, Polynesian culture; Mau Piailug.
n.certNote: Experts agree that Polynesians settled the Pacific on purpose, by skilled navigation. Exact dates for each island are still debated, and so is how much contact they had with South America.

d.try: On a clear night, with an adult, pick one bright star low on the eastern horizon and note what's under it, like a tree or a roof. Check again an hour later. The star will have risen and moved west. Polynesian navigators memorised where hundreds of stars rose and set, and used them like a compass.
myth: The Pacific islands were settled by accident, by people blown off course on drifting canoes.

Computer studies of winds and currents show drifting canoes would almost never reach distant islands like Hawaiʻi. Voyages like Hōkūleʻa's showed that Polynesians could sail there and back on purpose, using stars, waves and birds.
facts: Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa New Zealand and Rapa Nui (Easter Island)
from islands near New Guinea, about 3,000 years ago

sec.t:
The voyagers' ancestors came originally from Taiwan and the islands of South-East Asia. By about 3,000 years ago, a people known to archaeologists by their pottery, called Lapita, were sailing east from islands near New Guinea to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.

There they stayed for centuries, and Polynesian culture took shape. Then, around 1,000 years ago, a burst of long voyages carried people to the far corners of the triangle: Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa, settled around 1250 to 1300 CE.

sec.h: A star compass in the head
sec.t:
Navigators trained from childhood. They memorised where dozens of [[@constellations|stars]] rose and set on the horizon. Each star's rising point was like a house on a giant circle, a "star compass" kept in memory.

As one star climbed too high to use, the navigator switched to the next one rising at the same spot. By day, they steered by the Sun and by the swells. A swell is a long wave made by a far-off storm, which can keep a steady direction for days. Some navigators lay down in the hull to feel the [[@waves-how|waves]] crossing beneath them.

Signs of land helped close the gap. Clouds often pile up over islands, and lagoons can tint their undersides green. Floating plants, and seabirds heading home at sunset, also showed the way.

{{story:constellations}}

By the 20th century, many outsiders doubted Polynesians had sailed on purpose. Some thought they had simply drifted. In 1947, the Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl even argued they had come from South America, and drifted west on a raft called the *Kon-Tiki* to show it was possible.

In 1976, a group in Hawaiʻi built a replica double canoe called *Hōkūleʻa*. No Hawaiian navigator still knew the old methods, so they asked Mau Piailug, from the tiny Micronesian island of Satawal. Using no instruments, he guided the canoe about 4,000 km to Tahiti in about a month. Huge crowds met them on the beach.

Mau went on to teach Hawaiian navigators, and from 2014 to 2017 *Hōkūleʻa* sailed right around the world.

Polynesians grew the sweet potato, a plant from South America, long before Europeans arrived. And a DNA study published in 2020 suggested that some Polynesians and Native South Americans met around 800 years ago.

Who travelled to whom is still debated. Many experts think Polynesian sailors reached South America and came back, but the evidence isn't settled.

Across the Pacific, people are reviving traditional voyaging. Young navigators in Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa and Micronesia learn the star compass and sail long trips. The skills that once filled an ocean with people have become a source of pride. They are also a reminder that careful watching can [[@migration|find the way]] across a sea with no roads at all.

text: Los Angeles, often called LA, is the second-biggest city in the USA and the home of Hollywood, the American film industry. It is known for sunshine, beaches, long freeways and a skyline backed by mountains. Nearly 10 million people live in Los Angeles County (2024 estimate).

LA is also one of the most mixed cities in the world. People with roots in Mexico, [[@seoul|Korea]], the Philippines, China, Armenia, Iran, India and many other places live there, and more than 200 languages are spoken. It has hosted the Olympics twice and is due to host them again in 2028.

st.prompt: When the Hollywood sign went up in 1923, what was it for?

options.t: Advertising a new housing development
Celebrating the first film studio
Helping pilots find the airport

st.reveal: The sign said HOLLYWOODLAND and was put up to sell homes in the hills. It was meant to last only about a year and a half. In 1949 the last four letters were taken down, and it became a symbol of the film industry.

src: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, La Brea Tar Pits and Museum.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Los Angeles.

myth: The Hollywood sign has always said HOLLYWOOD.

sec.h: A small village by a river
sec.t:
Long before the city, the Tongva people lived in villages across the basin. In 1781, a group of 44 settlers came from New Spain, now Mexico, and founded a farming village near the Los Angeles River. They were of mixed Spanish, Indigenous and African roots. The village was named El Pueblo de la Reina de los Ángeles, the Town of the Queen of the Angels.

LA was part of Mexico until 1848, when it passed to the United States after a war. Railways, oranges and then oil helped it grow from a small town into a giant city in less than a century.

In the early 1900s, film companies started moving to Los Angeles from the east coast. The sun shone most of the year, which mattered when films needed natural light. Within a few hours' drive were beaches, deserts, mountains and forests, so one place could stand in for anywhere. Land was cheap, too.

By the 1920s, [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] was the centre of American film. The Hollywood sign, with letters about 14 m tall, was put up in 1923 to sell houses. Today studios in LA make films, TV shows and [[@animation-how|animation]] watched worldwide.

sec.h: Ice Age animals in the city

sec.t: LA spreads out over a huge area, and most people drive. Its freeways are famous for traffic jams. In the mid-1900s, exhaust from cars mixed with sunshine to form a brown haze called [[@fog-smog|smog]]. The mountains around the basin trap the air, making it worse. Strict rules on [[@cars-engine|car engines]] have greatly cleaned the [[@air-pollution|air]] since the 1970s, though LA still has bad days.

Los Angeles sits on many faults near the San Andreas Fault, so [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]] are common. The 1994 Northridge earthquake damaged freeways and buildings, and engineers learned lessons from it. Long dry seasons and hot winds called the Santa Anas also make the hills prone to [[@people-firefighters-forest|wildfires]]. In January 2025, large fires destroyed thousands of homes in and around the city.

On a hill above the city stands Griffith Observatory, opened in 1935. Anyone can look through its big telescope for free. From its terrace you can see the Hollywood sign on one side and, on a clear night, the whole city sparkling below.

text: The Narmada is one of the longest rivers of central India. It rises in the forests of Amarkantak in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]], runs about 1,312 km west and pours into the Arabian Sea near Bharuch in Gujarat.

People call it a lifeline because so much depends on it. Its water fills taps in cities such as Indore, waters farms across Gujarat and turns turbines that make electricity. For millions of Hindus it is also a holy river, often called Reva or simply Ma Narmada, "Mother Narmada".
Along the way it passes through three states, thick teak forests, marble gorges and wide fields of wheat and cotton. More than 40 smaller rivers join it before it reaches the sea.

st.prompt: Most big rivers of peninsular India flow east into the Bay of Bengal. Which way does the Narmada flow?

options.t: West, into the Arabian Sea
East, into the Bay of Bengal
North, into the Ganga

st.reveal: The Narmada flows west along a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges. Only a few large rivers, like the Narmada and the Tapi, take this westward path.

src: Government of India, Ministry of Jal Shakti, Narmada basin information.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Narmada River.

d.try: Fill a long baking tray with damp sand and press a ruler down the middle to make a groove. Tilt the tray slightly and pour water slowly at the high end. Watch how the water follows the groove, just as the Narmada follows its valley, and see where the sand it carries piles up.
myth: All the big rivers of India start in the Himalaya.
The Ganga, Yamuna and Brahmaputra do, but many great rivers start on the peninsula. The Narmada begins at Amarkantak, a plateau in central India about 1,000 m high.
facts: the Gulf of Khambhat, Arabian Sea

sec.t:
Look at a map of India and most peninsular rivers, like the Godavari and the Krishna, slope east toward the Bay of Bengal. The Narmada goes the other way. It flows through a [[@great-rift-valley|rift valley]], a long trough where blocks of the Earth's crust slipped down millions of years ago. The Vindhya hills rise to the north and the Satpura hills to the south, and the river is trapped between them.

Near Jabalpur, it has cut a gorge through soft white marble. At Bhedaghat the rock walls rise straight out of the water, and boats drift between them at night. A little upstream, the river crashes over Dhuandhar Falls in a cloud of spray, which is where the name, "smoke stream", comes from.

From the 1960s, governments planned about 30 large [[@dams-power|dams]] on the Narmada and its branches. The biggest is Sardar Sarovar in Gujarat, about 163 m tall at its highest point. Its canals carry water hundreds of kilometres into dry parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan, and it generates electricity for several states. The [[@statue-of-unity|Statue of Unity]] stands just downstream.

The dams also flooded forests and villages. Tens of thousands of families, many of them Adivasi farmers, had to move. From the 1980s a protest movement called the Narmada Bachao Andolan, "Save the Narmada", argued that people were not being treated fairly. Supporters of the dams pointed to the water and power they bring to drought-hit regions. Courts spent years weighing both sides, and people still disagree about whether the cost was worth it.

sec.h: Where the river meets the sea
sec.t:
By the time the Narmada reaches Bharuch, it is wide and slow. It drops its fine [[sediment|sediment]] into the Gulf of Khambhat, where the tides are among the strongest on India's coast. Fishermen here catch hilsa, the same silvery fish loved in Bengal.

Old bones turn up along the river too. In 1982, a geologist found part of an ancient human skull in its banks at Hathnora, one of the oldest human fossils known from India. Scientists still argue about its exact age, but most place it somewhere in the last few hundred thousand years. The same riverbanks have given up bones of giant elephants, hippos and wild cattle. The Narmada has been feeding people, and animals, for a very long time.

text: Cape Canaveral is a strip of sandy coast on the eastern side of Florida, in the USA. It is one of the busiest places in the world for launching rockets. People were sent to the Moon from here, along with Space Shuttles, Mars rovers and thousands of satellites.

Two neighbouring sites share the area. NASA's Kennedy Space Center sits on Merritt Island, and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station sits on the cape itself. Both government and private rockets launch from here, so a single week can see several launches. Around the launch pads lies a wildlife refuge, so rockets roar into the sky above alligators, sea turtles and wading birds.

st.prompt: Why do American rockets launch from Florida, rather than from somewhere like Alaska?

options.t: Florida is closer to the equator, so Earth's spin gives rockets a free push
Florida has less gravity
Rockets need hot weather to start their engines

st.reveal: Earth spins eastwards, and the ground near the equator moves fastest. At Cape Canaveral it is already moving at about 1,470 km/h, so rockets launched east get that speed for free. Launching east also sends them over the empty Atlantic Ocean.

src: NASA Kennedy Space Center, history and facilities.
US Space Force, Cape Canaveral Space Force Station history; US Fish and Wildlife Service, Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge.

d.try: Spin a ball on a string slowly, then let go and see where it flies. Now think of Earth spinning: a rocket launched eastwards starts with that sideways speed already. On a globe, find Cape Canaveral, Sriharikota in India and French Guiana, and see how close each is to the equator.
myth: Cape Canaveral and Kennedy Space Center are the same place.

They are neighbours. Kennedy Space Center, run by NASA, is on Merritt Island. Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, run by the US Space Force, is on the cape next door. Together people call the whole area the Space Coast.

sec.t:
Earth spins eastwards, and places near the equator move fastest. At Cape Canaveral, the ground is already moving east at about 1,470 km/h. A rocket launched eastwards keeps that speed, which saves fuel.

Florida also faces the Atlantic Ocean. Rockets fly east over open water, so any falling stages or failures land in the sea, far from towns. India uses the same idea at Sriharikota, which launches eastwards over the Bay of Bengal, as the story of [[@isro-launch|ISRO launches]] explains. Engineers choose [[@launch-sites|launch sites]] all over the world with these two rules in mind.

sec.h: From captured rockets to the Moon
sec.t:
The first launch from the Cape was on 24 July 1950. It was a rocket called Bumper 8, built partly from a German V-2 captured after the Second World War. Soon the Cape was busy with missile tests and then the space race.

On 16 July 1969, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Launch Complex 39A carrying Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. Four days later, two of them walked on the Moon. The Saturn V was 110 m tall, about as tall as a 36-storey building. You can follow that flight in [[@apollo-moon|Apollo and the Moon]].

For most of history, rockets were thrown away after one flight. Now the boosters of SpaceX's Falcon 9 often fly back and land upright, on pads near the coast or on ships at sea. Watching one return, with a double sonic boom, is a sight unique to the past decade. [[@reusable-rockets|Reusable rockets]] have made launches cheaper and much more frequent.

In 2025, Florida's Space Coast saw more than 100 launches, a record. The year before it had 93. Many of these carried batches of Starlink internet satellites.

On 1 April 2026, NASA's giant SLS rocket launched from Launch Complex 39B carrying the Artemis II crew. The four astronauts, three American and one Canadian, flew around the Moon and splashed down in the Pacific about nine days later. They were the first people to travel to the Moon since 1972.

Most of the land around Kennedy Space Center is a protected wildlife refuge. It is home to manatees, bobcats, sea turtles and hundreds of bird species. Bald eagles nest near launch pads. Alligators sometimes wander onto roads and runways, and staff have to wait for them to move. To learn how to tell them from their cousins, see [[@crocodiles-alligators|crocodiles and alligators]].

text: Sherlock Holmes is a made-up detective, one of the most famous characters in any book. The Scottish doctor and writer Arthur Conan Doyle created him in 1887. Holmes lives at 221B Baker Street in [[@london|London]] and solves crimes that baffle the police.

His method is simple to say and hard to do. He notices tiny details other people miss, such as a scuff on a boot, a stain on a sleeve or a smell of tobacco. Then he reasons his way from those clues to the one explanation that fits them all.
His friend Dr John Watson, an army doctor, narrates almost all the stories. Watson is clever too, but slower, which lets readers see how surprising Holmes's thinking really is.

st.prompt: In the very first story, what does Holmes work out about Dr Watson the moment they meet?

options.t: That he has just come back from Afghanistan
That he has a twin brother
That he has lost his wallet

st.reveal: Holmes says, "You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive." He notices Watson's tanned face, pale wrists, tired look and stiff, injured arm, and puts the clues together into one answer.

src: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Complete Sherlock Holmes (the four novels and 56 stories).
Britannica, Sherlock Holmes.
The Sherlock Holmes Museum, London, and the Arthur Conan Doyle Encyclopedia.

d.try: Play a Holmes game with a friend. Look carefully at their shoes, hands and school bag for one minute, then make three guesses about what they did that morning, giving a clue for each. Swap roles and see whose deductions hold up best.
myth: Sherlock Holmes often says "Elementary, my dear Watson."
The exact phrase never appears in Conan Doyle's stories. Holmes says "Elementary" once and "my dear Watson" often, but never together. The line became famous through later plays and films.

sec.t:
Conan Doyle was a young doctor with few patients and time to spare. He had studied at Edinburgh under a surgeon named Joseph Bell, who loved to guess where patients came from and what work they did just by looking at them. Doyle said Bell was a model for Holmes.

The first Holmes story, *A Study in Scarlet*, appeared in a Christmas magazine in 1887 and drew little notice. Things changed in 1891, when short Holmes stories began appearing in *The Strand Magazine*. People queued at newsstands for the next one. Each story was complete in itself, so a reader could pick up any issue and follow along. That was new, and it made both the magazine and its detective famous across Britain and the USA.

Conan Doyle grew tired of his detective. He wanted to be known for serious historical novels. So in "The Final Problem", published in 1893, Holmes wrestles his enemy Professor Moriarty and both seem to fall to their deaths at the Reichenbach Falls in [[@switzerland|Switzerland]].

Readers were furious. Doyle held out for years. Then came *The Hound of the Baskervilles*, a novel set before the fall, in 1901 and 1902. In 1903 Holmes properly returned, explaining that he had never gone over the edge at all. In the end there were four novels and 56 short stories.

Picture Holmes and you probably see a cape and a cap with flaps over the ears, called a deerstalker. Conan Doyle never named either one in the stories. The look came from Sidney Paget, the artist who drew Holmes for *The Strand*, and stage actors made it stick. The curved pipe came from the theatre too. In the books, Holmes plays the violin while he thinks, sometimes for hours.

Holmes inspired a whole family of [[@detective-stories|detective stories]]. In Bengal, Sharadindu Bandyopadhyay created Byomkesh Bakshi in the 1930s, a thinker who called himself a "truth-seeker" rather than a detective. Satyajit Ray later wrote about [[@satyajit-ray-stories|Feluda]], whose friend Topshe tells the stories much as Watson does, and Feluda openly admires Holmes.

Holmes has been played by hundreds of actors on stage, film and television, from Hollywood to Russia. Every week, a museum at 221B Baker Street, an address that didn't exist when Doyle wrote, welcomes visitors who come to see the home of a man who never lived.

text: You do. So does everyone else. English has no official office that approves new words. A word becomes real when enough people use it, for long enough, to mean the same thing.

Dictionary editors, called [[lexicographer|lexicographers]], don't invent words. They are more like word detectives. They collect examples from books, newspapers, websites and speech, and watch how a word spreads. When it has clearly settled into the language, it goes into the [[@dictionaries|dictionary]]. Big English dictionaries add hundreds of new words every year.
Some words have a famous inventor. Most have none. They just bubble up, often in playgrounds, games, songs and group chats, long before any grown-up writes them down.

sec.t:
Lewis Carroll loved making words. In his poem "Jabberwocky", from 1871, he wrote "chortle", a mix of chuckle and snort, and "galumph", a clumsy gallop. Both are in ordinary dictionaries now. He even explained his trick: squashing two words into one, which he called a portmanteau, after a kind of suitcase with two halves. His other inventions fill [[@alice-wonderland|Alice's Wonderland]].

Dr Seuss gave us the earliest known printed use of "nerd", in the book If I Ran the Zoo in 1950. There a nerd was just an odd little creature. In 2003 the Oxford English Dictionary added "muggle" from the Harry Potter books, for a person who lacks a skill.

Shakespeare is the earliest known writer of words like "eyeball" and "lacklustre". But many words once credited to him have turned up in older writing.

sec.h: Six ways to build a word
sec.t:
Most new words are made by a few simple tricks.

- Joining two words: sunflower, skateboard. - Blending parts of words: brunch (breakfast and lunch), smog (smoke and fog). - Borrowing from other languages. English took shampoo, bungalow, jungle and pyjamas from Indian languages, as you can see in [[@words-borrowed|words English borrowed]]. - Shortening: bus comes from omnibus, and maths from mathematics. - Using a name: the [[@food-sandwich-name|sandwich]] is named after an English earl. - Using initials as a word: laser and scuba started as long phrases.

Brand names can turn into words too. In 2006 "google" entered the Oxford English Dictionary as a verb.

Indian English has its own favourites, like "prepone", the opposite of postpone, and "timepass". In 2017 the Oxford English Dictionary added dozens of Indian English words, including "jugaad", meaning a clever, make-do fix, and "dabba".

That same year, Oxford Dictionaries chose "Aadhaar" as its first Hindi Word of the Year. A government ID scheme had turned a Sanskrit-rooted word meaning foundation into something every family talked about.

Young people have always driven new slang. In 2023 Oxford picked "rizz", meaning charm, as its Word of the Year, a word spread mostly by teenagers online.

There is even a famous children's novel about this. In Frindle, by Andrew Clements, a boy calls a pen a "frindle" to annoy his teacher, and the word spreads across America. And the strangest part? Real [[@slang|slang]] moves almost exactly the way that book describes.

text: [[@chillies|Chillies]] reached India from the Americas about 500 years ago, and Indian cooks soon made them their own. Their burn comes from a chemical called [[capsaicin|capsaicin]]. It doesn't mix with water, but it does dissolve in fat and oil. So water mostly sloshes it around your mouth.

Milk works better for two reasons. It contains fat, which can dissolve some capsaicin. And it contains a protein called casein, which acts a bit like soap. Casein grabs the oily capsaicin molecules, pulls them away from the nerve endings on your tongue and lets you swallow them. That is why curd, raita, lassi and buttermilk sit beside spicy meals all over India.

myth: Spicy food burns because it is actually damaging or heating your mouth.

sec.t:
Your mouth has tiny sensors on its [[@nervous-system|nerves]] that warn you about dangerous heat, like a too-hot cup of chai. Capsaicin fits into these sensors like a key in a lock and switches them on.

Your brain gets the message "fire!" even though nothing is hot. Your face may go red, your eyes may water and your nose may run. Some people even start to sweat, because the body tries to cool down from a heat that doesn't exist.

In the 1990s, the American scientist David Julius used capsaicin to find the exact sensor, called [[receptor|TRPV1]]. That discovery, about how we feel heat and touch, earned him a share of the Nobel Prize in 2021.

{{story:pain}}

Capsaicin is an oily molecule. Like oil and water in a salad dressing, it won't blend with water. A gulp of water washes over it and spreads it to fresh parts of your mouth, which can make the burn feel worse.

Ice-cold water can numb things for a few seconds, but the burn comes back once the water warms up. Fizzy drinks can make it worse, because the bubbles add their own prickle.

Milk is a mix of water, fat, sugar and proteins. Casein forms tiny clusters that are attracted to oily things. They surround capsaicin and drag it off the sensors.

A study at Penn State University in the USA tested several drinks after people sipped a spicy liquid. Milk worked best. Skimmed milk worked about as well as whole milk, which suggests the protein matters as much as the fat. Sugary drinks helped a bit too.

[[@curd-yogurt|Curd]], yoghurt, paneer and even a spoon of ghee can help in the same way. In South India, many meals end with curd rice, a cool, creamy finish after spicy dishes.

Chilli heat is measured in Scoville heat units. A bell pepper scores zero. A typical green chilli in an Indian kitchen may score a few thousand to tens of thousands.

The bhut jolokia, or ghost pepper, grown in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur, scores around 1 million. In 2007 it was named the world's hottest chilli. Since then, plant breeders in the USA have grown even hotter ones. As of 2023, the record belongs to Pepper X, at about 2.69 million units. Eating these can be risky, and people have ended up in hospital.

Mammals feel the burn of capsaicin, but birds don't. Their heat sensors are built slightly differently. A bird can eat the hottest chilli without blinking.

Scientists think this helps the chilli plant. Mammals chew and crush the seeds, but birds swallow them whole and drop them far away, ready to grow. Birds carry chilli seeds across forests and hills, one of many ways they spread plants, which is easier to understand once you see [[@how-birds-fly|how birds fly]].

text: Children everywhere love sweets, but what counts as a treat changes from place to place. In India it might be a gulab jamun or a piece of barfi. In Japan, a chewy mochi. In Brazil, a chocolate ball called a brigadeiro. In the United States, a bag of Halloween candy.

Many of these sweets are tied to festivals, family recipes and local farms. They use whatever grows nearby, such as rice in Japan, nuts in Turkey, milk in India and cocoa in the Americas. Together they tell a story about history, trade and celebration.

sec.t:
Sugarcane was first grown in New Guinea thousands of years ago. But turning its juice into dry crystals was worked out in India, more than 1,500 years ago. The Sanskrit word for the grains, sharkara, travelled through Persian and Arabic and became "sugar" in English. A lump of it, khanda, gave us "candy".

Traders carried [[@sugar|sugar]] along routes to the Middle East and Europe, where it was so costly it was called "white gold". Today it's cheap, which is why sweets are everywhere.

In [[@japan-culture|Japan]], families pound steamed sticky rice into soft mochi, especially at New Year. Some are filled with sweet red bean paste. Children also love dango, small rice balls on a stick, often glazed with a sweet soy sauce that tastes salty and sugary at once.

In Turkey and the Middle East, baklava layers paper-thin pastry with chopped nuts and honey or syrup. Spanish and Mexican children dip churros, long ridged doughnuts, into thick hot chocolate. In Argentina, dulce de leche, slowly cooked sweet milk, goes into almost everything.

Brigadeiros are small balls of condensed milk, cocoa and butter, rolled in chocolate sprinkles. A popular story says they were created in the 1940s and named after Brigadier Eduardo Gomes, who was running for president of Brazil. Today no Brazilian children's birthday party is complete without them. Children often help roll the sticky mixture into balls with buttered hands, which means a lot of licking of fingers.

In Australia, lamingtons, squares of sponge cake dipped in chocolate and rolled in coconut, are a school bake-sale favourite.

In 1897 a dentist named William Morrison and a sweet-maker named John C. Wharton came up with an electric machine that spun melted sugar into fine threads. They sold it as "Fairy Floss" at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis. Americans now call it cotton candy, and Indians often call it buddhi ke baal, or old lady's hair.

In the United States, [[@halloween|Halloween]] is a giant sweets festival. Children dress up and go door to door collecting chocolate bars and chewy candy. Indian children have their own sweet-filled festivals, from Diwali boxes of mithai to tilgul for Makar Sankranti.

Most sweets are mainly sugar, which feeds the germs that cause [[@sugar-teeth|tooth decay]]. Dentists suggest eating them with a meal rather than nibbling all day, and brushing well afterwards.
